publicado: Technical Product Manager | Quantitative Researcher | Data-Driven Risk & Growth Strategy | Building @AD.Trader
texto:
Most quant trading projects pour their resources into the execution layer and then die in the validation layer. The order should be reversed.

A working quantitative system is five layers: data, signal, strategy, execution, monitoring. Most people only see the middle one, so they spend serious engineering effort shaving milliseconds off order latency while an overfit curve runs underneath. Execution speed is only worth optimizing once the edge is confirmed real. Get the order wrong and faster just means losing money more efficiently.

▉ A backtest's job is to falsify, not to endorse

This is the least intuitive part. Most people treat a backtest as proof that an idea makes money, tuning parameters until the curve looks good. The right posture is the opposite: try every way you can to kill the strategy. Whatever survives is the only thing that might be a real edge.

Three gates at minimum: in-sample versus out-of-sample separation, walk-forward analysis, and the one most people skip, a multiple-testing penalty. Sweep a few hundred parameter sets and pick the best, and chance alone hands you a few that look strong. López de Prado's Deflated Sharpe Ratio taxes exactly that: the more combinations you tried, the more you should discount the best Sharpe you found. Skip it and your reported performance is almost certainly inflated.

▉ The friction band is a structural cost, not bad luck

Even after a strategy clears every statistical gate, slippage, fees, book depth, funding, and latency still sit between the backtest and live trading. Stacked together they can eat a thin edge whole. Run a pessimistic-cost backtest before going live: worst-case fees, worst-case slippage. If it still survives, it has earned real capital.

▉ Write the kill switch before you go live

No edge is permanent. Market structure shifts and the inefficiency you relied on gets arbitraged away. The question is never whether a strategy decays, but how fast you detect it. Define the failure conditions up front, turning the emotional call of whether to shut a strategy down into a rule you drew while still rational. That is what the monitoring layer is for.

Tools change. This order of questions does not. Whether each layer answers its own question matters far more than which language or framework you picked.

Which layer does your team most often underestimate?
